title: Ambulation and Mobility Assistance
path: Home Health Care Across the Lifespan

headings.title: Introduction to Mobility and Ambulation in Nursing
headings.content: Mobility is a fundamental aspect of human health, independence, and overall quality of life. In clinical and home healthcare settings, the nurse plays a central role in helping patients maintain, recover, or adapt their physical movement. Ambulation—the act of walking—is often used as a primary indicator of recovery after surgery, acute illness, or injury. When a patient loses the ability to move freely, multiple body systems begin to deteriorate rapidly. Nurses assess mobility baselines early to set realistic recovery goals and prevent the cascade of physiological decline associated with bed rest.

headings.title: Anatomical and Physiological Foundations of Movement
headings.content: Movement requires the coordinated interaction of the skeletal, muscular, and nervous systems. Bones provide the rigid framework and leverage points, skeletal muscles generate the force for contraction, and the nervous system provides precise timing and control through motor pathways. Proprioception—the body's ability to sense its position in space—allows smooth and balanced movement without constant visual monitoring. Any disruption in one of these components, such as nerve damage, muscle atrophy, or joint rigidity, directly impairs a patient's ability to walk or transfer safely.

headings.title: Comprehensive Nursing Assessment of Patient Mobility
headings.content: A thorough mobility assessment goes beyond simply asking if a patient can walk. Nurses evaluate muscle strength, joint range of motion, balance, gait, and tolerance for physical activity. Validated tools, such as the **Morse Fall Scale** or the **Timed Up and Go (TUG) test**, provide objective data regarding a patient's fall risk and functional capacity. Nurses also observe the patient during active movements to check for dizziness, shortness of breath, or pain, which may limit safe ambulation.

headings.title: Assistive Devices: Selection and Proper Use
headings.content:
When muscle weakness or balance deficits impair safe walking, assistive devices provide crucial support. Selecting the correct device depends on the patient's weight-bearing capacity, upper body strength, and cognitive status.

- **Canes**: Provide minimal support and balance assistance, held on the strong side of the body.
- **Walkers**: Offer a wide base of support for patients with significant balance issues, requiring adequate arm strength.
- **Crutches**: Used for temporary lower extremity injuries where partial or non-weight-bearing is prescribed.

headings.title: Techniques for Safe Transfers and Ambulation Assistance
headings.content: Moving patients between surfaces—such as from a bed to a chair—carries a high risk of injury for both the patient and the nurse. Proper body mechanics, including a wide base of support and keeping the load close to the body’s center of gravity, are mandatory. A **gait belt** should be applied securely around the patient's waist during ambulation to provide a safe grip point if the patient begins to fall. Nurses must also assess the path for obstacles and ensure non-slip footwear is worn before initiating any transfer.

headings.title: Preventing Complications of Immobility
headings.content:
Prolonged immobilization affects every major organ system, leading to predictable complications that nurses must actively prevent. 

| Body System | Immobility Complication | Nursing Prevention Strategy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integumentary | Pressure ulcers | Repositioning every two hours |
| Respiratory | Atelectasis and hypostatic pneumonia | Incentive spirometry and deep breathing |
| Cardiovascular | Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) | Early ambulation and compression stockings |
| Musculoskeletal | Contractures and muscle atrophy | Passive and active range of motion exercises |
